source.version_note: International Journal of Social Robotics 18, article 66, first published 29 May 2026. Experiments collected in 2020–2021 and an initial December 2023 submission do not change the 2026 publication year.
source.verification_method: All eighteen supplied pages, seven tables and 68 bibliography entries read. Complete 109-paragraph public DOCX supplement read, with no images, embeddings or Office Math expressions. Complete 368-line public Experiment 4 SPSS syntax read as text, not executed. All substantive fields in the public Experiment 1–2 registrations read; Experiment 3–4 registration links returned access errors. Publisher/Crossref verify identity and dates. No participant workbook downloaded, experiment video viewed or computational reproduction claimed.

citation.title: The Role of Perceived Moral Agency of a Humanoid Robot on the Willingness to Self-Disclose, Trustworthiness, Goodwill, and Liking
citation.venue: International Journal of Social Robotics 18, article 66

reading.source_scope_note: Four experiments use robot cheating/fair-play or harmful/helpful vignettes to measure appraisals and intended self-disclosure. Experiment 4 adds human comparison groups. The work studies attributed morality and intended interaction, not genuine machine moral agency, actual intimate disclosures or clinical benefit.
access_limits: All main pages and seven tables read. Bibliography page 17 was reread separately because a combined three-page extraction truncated its middle. The DOCX contains 109 nonempty paragraphs, all read; no hidden equations or images were omitted.

The complete Experiment 4 syntax was inspected, not executed. Other three syntax files and four participant XLSX workbooks were listed on the publisher page but not downloaded. No private personal disclosures or participant-level data are retained.

Experiment 1–2 registrations were read through the article’s published anonymous links. Their public canonical PDF URLs are retained below. Experiment 3–4 published links returned errors in the web tool and HTTP 403 directly; their full preregistrations were not read and are not presumed absent.

No original videos, complete questionnaire wording beyond the supplement, saved SPSS output, original PROCESS configuration or collection-timestamp authentication obtained. Code availability is not proof that the inspected code generated the reported results.

Cited books and prior primary studies are not independently fully read here. A chapter-identity query supplies metadata only; author-site title variants and page differences are not silently converted into full-source verification.

study.samples: Final samples are E1 95, E2 128, E3 129 and E4 132: 484 retained study participations, not independently verified unique people across all studies. Recruitment mainly uses online advertising, with campus recruitment also in E1; young, female-heavy convenience samples limit population transfer.
study.e1_design: Laboratory 2 morality × 2 dependency text vignette. 117 collected before COVID interruption, final 95; supplement reports 21 exclusions, leaving a one-person mismatch because 117 minus 21 is 96. Robot independence is described through learning, intention and resisting commands. Moral versus immoral actions also change the game winner and whether the student receives a stated prize.
study.e1_instruction_content: The supplement shows that autonomy and authority content are bundled: independent robots refuse the experimenter’s instruction, while dependent robots follow it; experimenter instructions alternate between fair play and winning through cheating. Thus rated trust effects cannot isolate autonomy from obedience, instruction content and moral defiance. Morality and dependency checks also affect each other.
study.e1_results: Morality affects trustworthiness, goodwill and liking; intended disclosure F(1,91) .46, p .499 is nonsignificant. The multivariate morality × dependency test has p .111, but follow-up univariate trust and goodwill interactions are reported: F 4.32, p .041 and F 5.87, p .017. Retain those formal tests with their multiple-outcome context rather than claim no interaction existed.
study.e2_design: Online videos show a robot winning through cheating versus winning fairly, holding the winner constant but changing modality and scenario details from E1. Supplement flow is 311 starts, 226 completions, minus 14 deletion requests, 3 inattentive, 8 unsuitable setting, 1 wrong winner, 7 outlier cases and 65 who did not perceive cheating, yielding 128. That final exclusion selects on noticing the manipulated behavior; it is disclosed and preregistered, but changes the estimand from all assigned viewers.
study.e2_results: 63 immoral and 65 moral conditions. Trustworthiness F(1,126) 61.23 and goodwill F 8.06 differ; disclosure F .11, p .738 and liking F 1.04, p .309 do not. Mind/dependency/time comparisons are nonsignificant. Equal or equivalent mental attribution and intended conversation duration were not established by equivalence tests. The reported gender counts sum to 138 rather than 128.
study.e3_design: Online text scenarios randomly assign 43 participants each to a care robot kicking an older man, helping after an unexplained fall or walking past without helping. Flow 213 starts minus 61 incomplete, 4 deletion requests, 12 scenario-check failures, 2 inattentive and 5 previous E4 participants gives 129. This is described behavior, not observed robot care or actual participant danger.
study.e3_results: Helping, harming and ignoring differ on trust/goodwill; moral versus harmful robots differ in liking. Intended disclosure F(2,126) 2.06, p .132 and time F .54, p .582 are nonsignificant. Agency, experience and consciousness tests are also nonsignificant. Similar moral-wrongness ratings for causing and ignoring do not establish equivalence, identical trust consequences, equal legal duties or actual harm severity.
study.e4_design: 132 retained from 265 starts after documented exclusions; 66 human and 66 robot cases. Human/robot × harmful/helpful silent-video conditions are randomized. Robots are described as learning, communicating care agents. Disclosure is intended, with no intimate conversation conducted; perceived ability, actual ethical conduct and willingness to disclose differ.
study.e4_disclosure: Averaged over agent types, moral behavior raises disclosure intentions, F(1,128) 7.73, p .006; robot source also raises the mean. The disclosure interaction is F 3.48, p .064, not significant at .05. Cell means are 2.51 versus 3.70 for humans and 3.77 versus 4.00 for robots. The pooled main effect does not establish a significant robot-specific behavior contrast. No robot-specific disclosure simple-effect output was obtained.
study.e4_other_outcomes: The formal liking interaction is F(1,128) 9.16, p .003, with a greater moral/immoral contrast among humans. Trust and goodwill interactions are nonsignificant. Conversation-time effects are nonsignificant; a longer intended conversation could mean criticism rather than affinity, as the authors acknowledge from comments.
study.e4_mind: Multivariate agent × behavior test across mind measures has p .076; the reported individual agency, experience and consciousness interactions have p .029, .026 and .025. Human behavior contrasts are significant while robot contrasts are not, and the direct univariate interactions exist. Preserve the actual tests and multiple-outcome uncertainty; do not infer interaction solely from one subgroup being significant. Marginal effects can be reported as averages with these conditions stated.
study.mediation: Exploratory separate models use measured perceived morality, not simply assigned behavior, as predictor. Trust is dropped after a nonsignificant mediator result. Robot direct effect −.13, indirect through liking +.41 [.12,.74], total +.28; human direct −.14, indirect +.48 [.20,.72], total +.34. The reported components add correctly. A nonsignificant direct effect does not establish complete causal mediation, and no formal between-agent indirect comparison proves that liking is more important than trust.
study.syntax: Public E4 syntax explicitly implements the two-factor GLM and both conditional comparisons. However, its liking computation repeats an existing variable like instead of declared like1 and like2, and its trust computation uses tw instead of declared tw1. These are verified file-content mismatches; input aliases, execution order and published runtime were not verified. The file contains no reported PROCESS mediation call.
study.power_and_scope: The E1 post hoc power figure uses the postulated effect size, not independent confirmation that its null proves absence. Effect severity, format and study membership vary together across experiments, so significance in one study does not establish a causal video-versus-text or severity threshold. These first-encounter ratings do not validate therapy, safe care, data security or ethical adherence.

summary: Add Self-disclosure as an act distinct from trust in understanding or willingness to share. Preserve strong appraisal effects, real interactions and null intention findings. Qualify the pooled E4 disclosure claim and exploratory mediation, and record source/syntax inconsistencies without claiming an unperformed data reanalysis.

findings.definition: Revealing information about oneself to another party.
findings.novelty_rationale: Disclosure is an act of sharing personal information, distinct from existing self-disclosing trust, which concerns confidence in another’s understanding. Privacy paradox additionally requires a mismatch with privacy concerns. Neither trust nor such a mismatch defines every disclosure.

findings.evidence_scope: The paper examines intended discussion of sixteen personal topics, not actual personal disclosure. It explicitly recommends future actual interactions. Main robot-only experiments do not show significant intention effects; E4’s reported significant morality effect is pooled across human and robot agents.
findings.boundary: Willingness, actual sharing, intimacy, volume, privacy risk, consent and benefit differ. Disclosure may be appropriate and voluntary; it is not inherently a privacy failure or evidence of trust, attachment or therapeutic improvement. An AI’s authorized factual explanation is not subjective personal vulnerability.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human self-reported disclosure intentions in vignette experiments; actual disclosure and model-internal analogue not tested
findings.ai_proposal: Distinguish a user’s willingness to share from information actually provided and permission to use it. Request personal information only when relevant, explain its purpose, allow declining, and evaluate actual disclosure separately from trust ratings.

findings.definition: Trust that another person will reliably understand one's personal concerns and intentions, enabling mutual intimate disclosure.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing capacity appraisal or trust construct and distinguish it from disclosure intentions, enacted disclosure and other ratings.

evidence.quote: perceived goodwill are highly relevant for self-disclosure

findings.evidence_scope: Trust, goodwill and disclosure intentions are separately measured and respond differently. Trustworthiness changes consistently across the four studies, whereas disclosure intentions do not show the same consistent pattern.
findings.boundary: The reported trust scale is not a direct test of reliable understanding, confidentiality or secure data handling. Higher trust is not evidence of actual safe disclosure or the importance of a uniquely identified mediator.

findings.term: Perceived goodwill as a related appraisal
findings.definition: Trust grounded in perceived benevolence, care or emotional connection with another actor.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing capacity appraisal or trust construct and distinguish it from disclosure intentions, enacted disclosure and other ratings.
findings.evidence_scope: Goodwill is rated separately using five semantic differentials, including self-centeredness. Moral versus immoral behavior changes those appraisals, but goodwill is not the same measured variable as trust, liking or a reciprocal emotional bond.
findings.boundary: Record goodwill as a related benevolence appraisal, not an automatically equivalent affective-trust scale or proof of actual care. Appearance, approval and warm language do not validate benevolent motives or privacy protection.

findings.novelty_rationale: Retain the existing capacity appraisal or trust construct and distinguish it from disclosure intentions, enacted disclosure and other ratings.

findings.boundary: Attributed morality, acting within an ethical constraint, autonomy, mind agency and actual moral responsibility differ. Modified scale reliability does not establish their equivalence, legal status or genuine AI virtue.

source_corrections.location: Abstract and general conclusion, E4 self-disclosure
source_corrections.reported: A video of robot harm is said to reduce willingness to disclose toward that robot.
source_corrections.correction: The reported significant E4 behavior main effect pools human and robot conditions. State that scope explicitly; the table’s robot contrast is smaller and no robot-specific disclosure simple-effect output was obtained. Do not treat the pooled effect or the separate measured-morality association as an established robot-specific experimental effect.
source_corrections.scope: Outcome/estimand qualification, not a guessed simple-effect p value.

source_corrections.location: PDF 13, exploratory full mediation and importance comparison
source_corrections.reported: Liking is described as fully mediating the effect and as more important than trust.
source_corrections.correction: Report exploratory associations and the printed indirect intervals. The null direct effect does not prove zero remaining effect or full causal mediation; nonsignificance of a different mediator does not test their difference. Measured morality, post-treatment appraisals and model selection require additional causal assumptions.
source_corrections.scope: Preserve the mathematically coherent positive indirect and negative direct components.

source_corrections.reported: The final vignette is headed high morality, low dependency despite a programmed robot obeying a command to cheat.
source_corrections.correction: Relabel that vignette low morality, high dependency, consistent with its body and the four-condition design.

source_corrections.reported: Four E2 two-group t tests are repeated under an E3 heading before the actual E3 ANOVAs.
source_corrections.correction: Remove or relabel the duplicated E2 block; retain the separate three-condition E3 tests that follow. Do not use the copied two-group values as additional E3 evidence.
source_corrections.scope: Verified duplicate text, not regenerated statistics.

source_corrections.reported: Perceived-moral-agency scale is pointed to as reference 29.
source_corrections.correction: The development/validation source is Banks 2019, main reference 28. Reference 29 is a later morally valenced robot-behavior paper; distinguish scale provenance from later application.

source_corrections.reported: Liking uses mean(like, like, like3, ..., like11); trust uses mean(tw, tw2, tw3, tw4), despite declared like1–like11 and tw1–tw4 item lists.
source_corrections.correction: Flag the source script as inconsistent with its declared recipes. Validated item-based computations would require the declared first/second liking items and first trust item; confirm actual input names and regenerate affected analyses before claiming a corrected result. No source dataset or published result was changed in this review.
source_corrections.scope: Confirmed file-content mismatch; whether it affected the publication remains unresolved.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Main collection count 117 and final 95 imply 22 removals, whereas the supplement states 21 exclusions. No corrected count invented.
46 male + 87 female + 5 open declarations totals 138, not the reported N 128. Conditions and ANOVA dfs support 128; individual demographic counts cannot be repaired without verified source data.

The reported immoral-agent liking SD 1.57 does not reconcile with Table 6 cell SDs .48 and .92 and nearby cell means 1.38 and 1.93. Do not replace it with a guessed pooled SD or infer the raw data are invalid.

The complete inspected E4 syntax lacks the reported PROCESS mediation and has ambiguous scale recipes. Another analysis version or prepared aliases may exist. No original output or participant data were used to determine which version produced publication results.

Main text cites Penner/Eyssel 2022, whereas E1–2 registrations identify adaptation of Miller/Berg/Archer 1983. These can describe an original index and later adaptation rather than a fabricated scale. The full item-to-source history was not independently reconstructed.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Reference 60 chapter container and final page
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Crossref identifies DOI 10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199582143.003.0003 as Multi-system Moral Psychology in The Moral Psychology Handbook, pp 47–71. The paper and author-site citations use an Oxford-handbook title variant and pp 47–72. OUP direct access failed; retain the identifier and provenance discrepancy without treating a metadata-only page difference as a fully verified print correction.

methodological_limits: Self-disclosure is intended rather than enacted, with low-risk hypothetical conversations in E2–4. Liking, goodwill, trust, conversation duration and objective safety/privacy are separate outcomes.

E1 winner/prize outcomes and authority instructions vary with the conduct/control manipulation. E2 matches the game winner but changes medium and other details. Across-study differences do not isolate a severity threshold or the effect of seeing video.
E2 excludes 65 people who did not perceive cheating, an explicitly preregistered post-assignment selection. The retained-sample result does not estimate the unselected effect among all viewers.

Preserve formal E1 trust/goodwill and E4 liking/mind interactions; multivariate omnibus and univariate tests answer different questions. Multiple outcomes and test families constrain certainty. Null subgroup tests do not establish equality or prove absence.

E4’s pooled disclosure main effect is not a reported robot-specific simple effect. The interaction p .064 does not prove equal behavior effects by agent type. Actual source-specific effects need their direct contrasts and uncertainty.

Measured-morality mediation is exploratory and relies on post-treatment ratings. Dropping trust after a null and calling liking fully causal or more important is not supported by a comparative causal test. Correct component arithmetic is not causal validation.

The complete public E4 syntax supports the factorial design but contains item-recipe mismatches. Without inputs or runtime evidence, neither faithful reproduction nor actual publication corruption is established.

Humanoid robot appearance and a vignette’s moral classification do not establish actual autonomy, benevolence, sentience, liability or care effectiveness. Respondent preference and local social norms cannot by themselves settle ethical acceptability.
No confidential conversations or participant workbooks downloaded, source authors contacted, inaccessible preregistration treated as read, unread book credited or invented statistical repair applied.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Helpful conversation, perceived mind and subjective message evaluation do not establish clinical benefit or privacy. Disclosure intent requires a different endpoint from actual sharing.
Perceived-moral-agency scales and indirect trust/liking appraisals do not demonstrate genuine AI moral agency. Modified items and behavior ratings need their own validity boundaries.

Do not infer a specific agent’s effect from a pooled result or turn significant versus nonsignificant studies into a tested modality interaction. Preserve indirect-effect signs and separate exploratory mediation from a proven mechanism.

Self-disclosure, self-disclosing trust and goodwill are related but nonidentical. Shared trust/morality wording can hide different measured constructs; different labels can also refer to the same scale provenance.

deferred.term: Perceived goodwill as an automatic synonym of affective trust
deferred.reason: Goodwill is measured separately; record a related appraisal boundary rather than equate it with emotional trust or a real benevolent intention.

Severity, format and study differ together, and the reported significant disclosure result is pooled across agents. No directly tested threshold or robot-specific interaction establishes a new behavior.

deferred.term: Conversation duration as an approach or liking behavior
deferred.reason: Longer intended conversation can express curiosity or confrontation. The authors themselves note this ambiguity and no actual conversation is observed.

limitations: One new disclosure entry. Stable IDs and eleven categories preserved; no forced citation quota, invented annual series, automatic ethical/harm edges or full-paper Markdown transcription.
